newsitem.title: POLAND: Satisfied Poles thank Clinton for NATO.
newsitem.headline: Satisfied Poles thank Clinton for NATO.

text.p: Poles from President Aleksander Kwasniewski all the way down to revellers in Warsaw's Castle Square applauded U.S. President Bill Clinton on Thursday for setting them firmly on the road to security in NATO.

"We thank President Clinton and the whole White House administration for their determination in securing this historic decision in Madrid," Kwasniewski's spokesman quoted him as telling Clinton in Warsaw's presidential palace.

Clinton came straight to Poland after this week's NATO summit in Spain when the Western alliance invited Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary to start entry negotiations leading to planned admission in 1999.
Having picked Warsaw as the place to congratulate the successful candidates, Clinton is travelling to Romania on Friday to reassure the states left out for now.
U.S. National Security Adviser Samuel Berger quoted Kwasniewski as saying: "This is a decision that changes the history of Europe and the world."
Clinton and Kwasniewski were later due to speak to thousands of Poles celebrating to the sound of folk and country music of both countries on Warsaw's Castle Square.
Berger told reporters Clinton had said the credit for Poland's admission lay with its people's past struggles for democracy.
It was in Poland that Solidarity in 1980 won recognition as the Soviet bloc's first free trade union, giving teetering Soviet power a push that helped bring its collapse in 1989.
Clinton was scheduled to meet the pre-1989 Solidarity leader Lech Walesa who as Polish president pushed hard for NATO admission during Clinton's previous Polish trip in 1994.

Clinton was also bringing a message that the three states must shoulder their share of the financial and other burdens of NATO entry -- which in Poland's case will eventually mean a costly modernisation of its 230,000-strong army.

Kwasniewski, whose ex-communist ruling allies face a challenge from Solidarity in elections on September 21, told Clinton Poland's main strategic aims would remain unchanged and its economic reforms would continue whoever won.

He said Poland would aim to exert a positive influence throughout the region and cooperate with Russia. "We don't want to build a structure of European security against Russia," spokesman Antoni Styrczula quoted him as saying.
Berger said the presidents discussed the responsibilities NATO membership would impose on Poland, including financial costs, but he said no specific figures had been mentioned.
Clinton has stressed that NATO's growth has to be ratified by legislatures of all 16 current members including the United States, where two-thirds of senators will have to approve it next year.
Many Americans have doubts about the cost to U.S. taxpayers or the wisdom of antagonising Russia, so Clinton's visit was also intended as a nudge to U.S. public opinion.

Poland fell to German and Soviet invasion in 1939, and following World War Two it was left to Soviet control by London and Washington -- a history that makes 80 percent of Poles want to join NATO and most of them desire European Union entry too.
Among those on Castle Square was Jozef Koronowski, 70, who said he had survived the Nazi concentration camp at Sachsenhausen in World War Two and had been liberated by the U.S. army.

"It is a powerful army and it's good to have such allies. I am very happy Poland will be in NATO and President Clinton is here to tell us this. Now we can sleep easily," Koronowski told Reuters. "There will be no more deportations to Siberia."
